RagShortTexts: Prices, tolls and transport shaped trading at Krakow’s market.

Variants.Content: Kraków served as the seniorate capital of Poland, and Wawel Castle rose above the Vistula on its limestone bluff. The city's great market was anchored by the Sukiennice Cloth Hall, which gathered the cloth and goods of Europe into one place. The castle had been rebuilt after the Mongol raid of 1241, and its stone walls stood as a symbol of Piast continuity during an age of ducal fragmentation. Each Piast duke who held the seniorate claimed the castle as his seat, and each rival duke measured his own power against it. Tolls on the river and the market fees paid for the city's walls and garrison, so the royal treasury depended on the trade that passed through its gates.

The martyred Saint Stanislaus lies enshrined in Wawel Cathedral. Piast faithful believe that just as the martyr's severed limbs miraculously re-fused, fractured Polish duchies will one day reunite into a single kingdom. The saint was canonized in 1253, and his cult made the cathedral the chief shrine of the realm. Clergy who served the altar kept the relics and tended the pilgrims.

Farmers visiting Krakow compared the prices of salt, cloth and grain. The market laid out after the 1257 charter offered stalls and opportunities, but homespun linen might not pay for imported woolens. Tolls, carriage and road security shaped the proceeds, with money still needed for seed and household goods.
